newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS-Romania, seeking IMF loans, passes budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Romania, seeking IMF loans, passes budget.

text.p: Romania's parliament approved the 1997 state budget on Thursday, a key plank of the new centrist government's push to win fresh western credits ahead of an International Monetary Fund meeting next week.
Parliament approved the law by 230 votes to 157 after a week of debate under emergency procedures. Leftists, thrown out of office in last November's election, and nationalists voted against.

"Parliament has understood that delaying the budget creates problems for social projects and that we cannot leave the country without money," Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said in the final stages of debate.

The IMF is to decide on restoring credits for Romania at a Board meeting on April 23 and saw the budget and the progress of market reforms as a pre-condition for approval. The Fund is considering loans of about $400 million, which would pave the way for a further $600 million in credits from the World Bank.
The government has made plain its reformist credentials by announcing plans to pass 40 pieces of legislation to speed privatisation and restructure oversize communist-era industry.
A bank selloff bill is to clear parliament on Friday, while amendments to foreign investment, banking and land leasing bills are expected to get cabinet approval within days.

Opposition leaders accused the new ruling coalition of failing to meet campaign promises to raise the living standards of Romanians, who earn an average of $80 per month, to those of neaqrby ex-communist Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

"The adoption of the budget represents the victory of the government against the country," Adrian Nastase, First Vice President of the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), told the session of parliament's two chambers.

Ciumara retorted that the PDSR had squandered decades worth of budget revenues while in power. It was incomprehensble, he said, to vote against the budget "and leave children without benefits and pensioners without pensions".

Under the law, the state budget deficit was set at 12.6 trillion lei ($1.8 billion) or 5.4 percent of gross domestic product, which is expected to contract by three percent after growth of 4.1 percent in 1996.
It also provided for the consolidated budget deficit to be trimmed to 4.5 percent of GDP from 5.8 percent last year. That figure was nearly three times over targets set with the IMF.
Inflation is forecast at a year-on-year rate of 90 percent despite reaching 76.5 percent in the first quarter after unrealistic prices for staples and utilities were freed.
The IMF has acknowledged that the inflation forecast is too ambitious and many economists say it will have to be revised along with the entire budget this summer.
Latest government statistics put the state budget deficit at about 340 billion lei for the first two months of the year.
Taking account of inflation, that figure reflected cautious expenditure compared to last year's figure of 311 billion.
The IMF gave its backing to proposed indicators in talks with ministers launched immediately after last November's election victory by the centrists.
The Fund suspended credits to Romania last year after criticising the leftist administration's spending record and restrictions on foreign exchange markets. ($=7,063 lei)
